title: Chanakya and the Hot Porridge
text:
Chanakya, also called Kautilya, is remembered in Indian tradition as the brilliant and ruthless Brahmin who helped the young Chandragupta Maurya overthrow the Nanda dynasty of Magadha and found the Maurya empire in the late 4th century BC. Many legends gathered around him, preserved in later Buddhist and Jain writings.

One of the best known appears in the Jain poet Hemachandra's account and, in a somewhat different form, in a Buddhist commentary on the chronicle of Sri Lanka. In Hemachandra's version, Chanakya and Chandragupta first attacked the Nanda capital directly and were badly beaten. They had to flee and wandered the country in disguise.

One day they were in a village and overheard a mother scolding her child. The boy had been given a bowl of hot rice porridge and had put his fingers straight into the middle, burning himself. The mother told him that he was as foolish as Chanakya, who attacked the center of the kingdom first. Eat from the edges, she said, where it has cooled, and work your way inward.

Chanakya took the lesson. Instead of striking the capital, he and Chandragupta built up their forces by winning over the frontier regions first, then advanced step by step. In the legend, they closed in on the Nanda center only when the outer lands were theirs, and Chandragupta became king.
lesson: When the center of a problem is too hot to handle, start at the edges. Build strength where resistance is weakest and close in once you have a base.
source: Hemachandra, Parishishtaparvan, canto 8; Vamsatthappakasini (Pali commentary on the Mahavamsa)
caveat: The story is a legend preserved in sources written many centuries after the events.
